Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Vulnerable google-cloud-aiplatform SDK install (CVE-2026-2473 — pre-1.148.0) AIWeaponization High
Detects installation or invocation of google-cloud-aiplatform Python SDK at versions 1.139.0 through 1.147.x, which silently fall back to an attacker-owned GCS bucket via the deterministic `<project>-vertex-staging-<location>` pattern when no explicit staging bucket is supplied. Catches both first-time installs and runtime use of vulnerable libraries that should be upgraded to ≥1.148.0. Rationale: Pins to the EXACT vulnerable SDK version range disclosed in the Unit 42 article (1.139.0 — 1.147.x; fixed in 1.148.0 released 2026-04-15). The version regex eliminates noise from already-patched installs. Catches both interactive pip installs and CI/CD pipelines pulling pinned vulnerable versions. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://pypi.org/project/google-cloud-aiplatform/#history
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data science teams legitimately running pinned but outdated SDK versions in research notebooks
  • CI/CD pipelines re-installing an old pinned version in lockfiles awaiting upgrade
  • Docker image rebuilds replaying historical pip install commands from cached layers
  • Developers reproducing a known issue against a specific old SDK version for support tickets
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("docker.exe","buildkitd.exe") and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--dry-run","download","--no-deps"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/user and pull the full pip-install context — is this a developer workstation, build agent, or production ML pipeline? Check whether the SDK is actively used (search for `aiplatform.Model.upload` calls in the same project). 2) Contain: force-upgrade google-cloud-aiplatform to ≥1.148.0 in the affected environment; if the host has uploaded models in the last 7 days, treat any default-named staging buckets as suspect and verify ownership via `gcloud storage buckets describe`. 3) Hunt: pivot to GCS audit logs for any bucket matching `<project-id>-vertex-staging-<location>` and confirm the bucket resides in the customer's own project, not an attacker-controlled one. Check Vertex AI Model Registry for models uploaded during the vulnerable window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","pip","pip3","python","python3")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "google-cloud-aiplatform"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"google-cloud-aiplatform==1\.(139|140|141|142|143|144|145|146|147)\."
| extend VulnerableVersion = extract(@"google-cloud-aiplatform==(1\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountUpn, VulnerableVersion, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "pip.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "pip3.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "python.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "python3.exe"
| where CommandLine has "google-cloud-aiplatform"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"google-cloud-aiplatform==1\.(139|140|141|142|143|144|145|146|147)\."
| extend VulnerableVersion = extract(@"google-cloud-aiplatform==(1\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, CommandLine)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, SubjectUserName, VulnerableVersion, CommandLine, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vertex AI default staging bucket squatting — predictable bucket pattern access AIDelivery Medium
Hunts GCP audit logs for storage operations on buckets matching the deterministic `<project-id>-vertex-staging-<location>` pattern where the acting identity is NOT the customer's Vertex AI P4SA (`service-<project-num>@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com`) or a known internal pipeline service account. Surfaces both cross-tenant bucket squatting and unexpected writes that could be model-artifact poisoning. Rationale: Targets the exact bucket-name pattern from the article (`staging_bucket_name = project + "-vertex-staging-" + location`). Filtering OUT the legitimate Vertex AI P4SA isolates the access path the attacker would use — either bucket-squatting from a different project or an unexpected internal principal touching the staging bucket. Sigma omitted because this requires aggregation/exclusion logic not expressible as single-event-shape. Falcon/Defender/CloudWatch empty because this is GCP-native telemetry with no Falcon FDR or Microsoft endpoint equivalent. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/service-agents
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1525 T1530
Data sourcesWeb Change
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Customer DevOps service account legitimately reading the staging bucket during pipeline orchestration
  • Terraform/IaC service account creating or auditing the bucket during infra provisioning
  • Cloud Storage Transfer Service or Backup service principals enumerating buckets
  • Internal user using `gcloud storage` CLI for ad-hoc model artifact inspection
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm bucket ownership with `gcloud storage buckets describe gs://<bucket>` — if the project_number doesn't match your project, you've been squatted; treat as confirmed. Inventory any model artifacts already staged there. 2) Contain: immediately delete and recreate the bucket explicitly under your project, then upgrade the SDK to ≥1.148.0 across all clients. Revoke any models uploaded during the vulnerable window from the Vertex AI Model Registry and redeploy from a verified source. 3) Hunt: pull Vertex AI deployment events for the affected region and inspect model artifacts (`gsutil cat gs://<bucket>/.../model.joblib | python -c 'import pickletools; pickletools.dis(...)'`) for `__reduce__` payloads. Check IAM audit logs for any new permissions granted to external principals.
GCPAuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ServiceName == "storage.googleapis.com"
| extend BucketName = extract(@"projects/_/buckets/([^/]+)", 1, tostring(ResourceName))
| where BucketName matches regex @"-vertex-staging-(us|europe|asia|australia|northamerica|southamerica)"
| extend Principal = tostring(AuthenticationInfo.principalEmail)
| where Principal !endswith "@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Methods=make_set(MethodName), Principals=make_set(Principal), EventCount=count() by BucketName
| order by LastSeen desc
source:gcp.audit @protoPayload.serviceName:storage.googleapis.com @protoPayload.resourceName:*-vertex-staging-* -@protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail:*@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com
CLOUD
`gcp_audit_logs` data.protoPayload.serviceName="storage.googleapis.com"
| rex field=data.protoPayload.resourceName "projects/_/buckets/(?<bucket_name>[^/]+)"
| where match(bucket_name, "-vertex-staging-(us|europe|asia|australia|northamerica|southamerica)")
| eval principal=data.protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail
| where NOT match(principal, "gcp-sa-aiplatform\.iam\.gserviceaccount\.com$")
| stats min(_time) as firstSeen max(_time) as lastSeen values(data.protoPayload.methodName) as methods values(principal) as principals count by bucket_name
| `security_content_ctime(firstSeen)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastSeen)`

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

China-Linked SprySOCKS Backdoor Expands to Windows with Driver-Based Stealth

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 10 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged two previously undocumented Windows variants of what was believed to be a Linux-only backdoor called SprySOCKS. "The Windows variants discovered are internally marked as WIN_DRV and WIN_PLUS," ESET said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "Both come with a hard-coded C&amp;C [command-and-control] configuration and support communication over TCP, UDP,

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] CVE-2023-24932 exposure surface — UEFI bootkit pre-OS attack risk
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] WIN_PLUS Print Spooler abuse: spoolsv.exe spawns svchost.exe
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SprySOCKS WIN_DRV kernel driver file dropped (KW1B/KX1B *.dat) · [LLM] Kernel driver service registered with SprySOCKS WIN_DRV ImagePath · [LLM] Suspicious Print Processor registry persistence (WIN_PLUS T1547.012) · [LLM] WIN_DRV chain: scheduled task creation followed by SprySOCKS driver drop · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
SprySOCKS WIN_DRV kernel driver file dropped (KW1B/KX1B *.dat) AIInstallation High
Hunts the on-disk drop of the two named SprySOCKS WIN_DRV kernel components — RawWNPF (KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat) and DriverLoader (KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat). These exact filenames are unique to the FishMonger/Earth Lusca Windows port and have no legitimate use; a single hit is a confirmed compromise. Rationale: Filenames KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat (RawWNPF) and KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat (DriverLoader) are named verbatim in the ESET writeup and the Hacker News summary. Regex anchor on the K[WX]1B5206BDC1743(FP|DD).dat family catches any minor naming-permutation observed across the campaign while keeping FP rate ~zero. Cross-checked against ESET WeLiveSecurity, Security Affairs, and Bleeping Computer reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/ • https://securityaffairs.com/193728/apt/china-linked-fishmonger-ports-sprysocks-to-windows-with-kernel-level-stealth-and-uefi-bootkit-hints.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/windows-version-of-sprysocks-linux-malware-used-to-attack-govt-orgs/
ATT&CKT1014 T1543.003 T1547.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • EDR/AV vendor sandbox detonation of the sample inside the corporate estate
  • Incident-response analyst manually staging the sample for reverse engineering
  • Threat-intel platform automatically downloading the sample for enrichment
  • Backup or forensic image restore replaying historical infected file events
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe", "MpCmdRun.exe", "CSFalconService.exe", "SentinelAgent.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull DeviceFileEvents for the host — confirm the writing process (likely a side-loaded DLL or scheduled-task spawn), grab SHA256 of both writer and dropped file, check if a kernel service was registered under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\* pointing at the .dat. Step 2 (contain): isolate the device via Defender/Crowdstrike network isolation immediately; do NOT reboot — driver-based stealth means kernel hooks unload only on reboot and you want a live memory snapshot first. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the writing process SHA256 across the estate, check DeviceProcessEvents for spoolsv.exe→svchost.exe chains (WIN_PLUS variant), and DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound TCP/UDP/WebSocket from suspect processes; expand search backwards 90 days as the campaign ran 2023-2024.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^K[WX]1B5206BDC1743(FP|DD)\.dat$"
   or FileName in~ ("KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat", "KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^K[WX]1B5206BDC1743(FP|DD)\.dat$"
   or TargetFileName in~ ("KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat", "KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/(KW1B5206BDC1743FP|KX1B5206BDC1743DD)\.dat$/i

Kernel driver service registered with SprySOCKS WIN_DRV ImagePath AIInstallation High
Detects registry writes that register a Windows service whose ImagePath references the SprySOCKS WIN_DRV driver components (KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat / KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat). This is the kernel-driver persistence anchor for the RawWNPF rootkit and DriverLoader chain. Rationale: The article describes RawWNPF (KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat) and DriverLoader (KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat) as kernel drivers; on Windows kernel drivers must be registered as services under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<name>\ImagePath. Matching the article-specific filename family in the ImagePath value is article-specific and effectively zero-FP. Cross-referenced ESET WeLiveSecurity report. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/ • https://gbhackers.com/sprysocks-windows-backdoor-uses-kernel/
ATT&CKT1547.006 T1543.003 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security tool re-detonation of the sample in a managed sandbox VM
  • DFIR engineer staging the driver for offline analysis on a workstation
  • Forensic acquisition / VM-restore replaying historic infected registry hives
  • Threat-intel platform's auto-sandbox ingesting the binary
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): capture the InitiatingProcess + parent that wrote the registry value; correlate with DeviceFileEvents for the corresponding .dat file drop and DeviceProcessEvents for the writing process tree (look for batch script → schtasks → DLL side-loader as the parent chain). Step 2 (contain): isolate the host BEFORE reboot — the driver is kernel-resident and a reboot loses live state; collect a memory image (winpmem / volatility) of the device, then disable the service via offline registry edit. Step 3 (hunt): sweep all hosts for the service-name and ImagePath patterns; check HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Environments\*\Print Processors\ for the WIN_PLUS sister persistence; review outbound TCP/UDP/WebSocket on the impacted device — kernel rootkit hides the listening port so look for unexpected established sockets from svchost.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet", "RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "ImagePath"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("KW1B5206BDC1743FP", "KX1B5206BDC1743DD")
   or RegistryValueData matches regex @"(?i)K[WX]1B5206BDC1743(FP|DD)\.dat"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("RegistryValueSet", "RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
| where RegistryValue =~ "ImagePath"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("KW1B5206BDC1743FP", "KX1B5206BDC1743DD")
   or RegistryValueData matches regex @"(?i)K[WX]1B5206BDC1743(FP|DD)\.dat"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WIN_PLUS Print Spooler abuse: spoolsv.exe spawns svchost.exe AIExploitation High
Detects the WIN_PLUS execution chain where the Print Spooler service (spoolsv.exe) loads a malicious first-stage print processor that creates and injects into a new svchost.exe to launch the SprySOCKS backdoor. spoolsv.exe spawning svchost.exe is virtually never seen in benign telemetry — svchost is normally spawned by services.exe. Rationale: Article explicitly states 'WIN_PLUS execution scheme... leverages the Windows Print Spooler service (spoolsv.exe) as a starting point... designed to inject and run a SprySOCKS loader into a newly created svchost.exe process.' The parent-child pair spoolsv.exe→svchost.exe has effectively zero benign baseline (svchost is always spawned by services.exe in normal Windows operation). Verified against ESET WeLiveSecurity report. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/ • https://www.darkreading.com/threat-intelligence/sprysocks-windows-variant-kernel-drivers • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/windows-version-of-sprysocks-linux-malware-used-to-attack-govt-orgs/
ATT&CKT1055.012 T1547.012 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Niche third-party print driver installers that briefly spawn svchost during printer registration
  • Defender / EDR sandbox detonation of the actual SprySOCKS sample
  • Windows Update servicing stack patching the Print Spooler binary (very rare)
  • Manual Print Spooler debugging session by an engineer running attached to spoolsv
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("setup.exe", "msiexec.exe", "TrustedInstaller.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the full process tree (grandparent → parent → svchost child) and the child svchost's loaded DLLs (DeviceImageLoadEvents) — look for unsigned or non-System32 DLLs and any new print processor DLL loaded by spoolsv just prior. Step 2 (contain): isolate the host pre-reboot; collect memory; suspend the svchost child PID to preserve injected code before kernel rootkit (WIN_DRV companion) potentially hides it. Step 3 (hunt): query DeviceRegistryEvents for any new value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Environments\*\Print Processors\ on the impacted host and across the estate; correlate against DeviceFileEvents for KW1B/KX1B *.dat drops indicating the WIN_DRV sibling is also resident.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "spoolsv.exe"
| where FileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentFolder = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentSHA256 = InitiatingProcessSHA256,
          ChildFolder = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          ChildSHA256 = SHA256,
          GrandparentName = InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "spoolsv.exe"
| where TargetProcessName has "svchost.exe" or ActingProcessName has "svchost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Suspicious Print Processor registry persistence (WIN_PLUS T1547.012) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of a non-default Print Processor entry under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Environments\*\Print Processors\, the WIN_PLUS persistence anchor that causes spoolsv.exe to autoload the first-stage SprySOCKS loader DLL at every boot. Default benign processor is winprint.dll — anything else is rare and suspicious. Rationale: Article: 'WIN_PLUS execution scheme... leverages the Windows Print Spooler service (spoolsv.exe)... to execute a first-stage loader that runs as a print processor.' The print-processor MITRE technique (T1547.012) requires a Driver value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Environments\<arch>\Print Processors\<name>\ — by default this is winprint.dll. Any other DLL is rare enough to alert on. Validated via ESET writeup and Cybersecurity News which call out 'print processor registry abuse' explicitly. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/fishmonger-hackers-expands-sprysocks-backdoor-from-linux/
ATT&CKT1547.012 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate third-party print driver installation (Canon, Xerox, Konica, HP enterprise drivers occasionally register custom processors)
  • Print management software (PaperCut, Equitrac) installing receipt-print processors
  • Windows feature install for advanced print servers in print server roles
  • XPS / PDF virtual-printer installation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe", "TrustedInstaller.exe", "setup.exe", "PrintInstaller.exe", "Pcounter.exe", "papercut-mf-server.exe", "papercut-print-deploy-client.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains @"\Program Files\Canon\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains @"\Program Files\Xerox\"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the InitiatingProcess + parent for the registry write — installer process from a print-vendor MSI is a likely benign root cause; an unsigned binary in user-writable paths or a script interpreter is malicious. Pull DeviceFileEvents to find the DLL being referenced and check its signer/hash. Step 2 (contain): if DLL signer is missing/invalid or DLL path is in %ProgramData%/%Public%/%Temp%, isolate the host BEFORE rebooting and acquire memory; remove the registry value via offline edit. Step 3 (hunt): for the suspect DLL hash, sweep for additional hosts; query DeviceFileEvents for the WIN_DRV sibling .dat drops (KW1B/KX1B pattern); correlate against DeviceProcessEvents for spoolsv.exe→svchost.exe spawns.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet", "RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\Control\Print\Environments\"
| where RegistryKey contains "Print Processors"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "Driver"
| where RegistryValueData !endswith "winprint.dll"
| where isnotempty(RegistryValueData)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("RegistryValueSet", "RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\Control\Print\Environments\"
| where RegistryKey contains "Print Processors"
| where RegistryValue =~ "Driver"
| where RegistryValueData !endswith "winprint.dll"
| where isnotempty(RegistryValueData)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Default Print Processor Registered - SprySOCKS WIN_PLUS
id: 3d7e9f1a-8c5b-4e2d-a6f1-5b3c8d4e7a1c
status: experimental
description: Detects registration of a print processor whose Driver value is not the default winprint.dll - SprySOCKS WIN_PLUS uses Print Processor autoload for persistence.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\Control\\Print\\Environments\\*\\Print Processors\\*" Registry.registry_value_name="Driver" Registry.registry_value_data!="winprint.dll" by Registry.dest Registry.user Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data Registry.process_name Registry.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
WIN_DRV chain: scheduled task creation followed by SprySOCKS driver drop AIInstallation Medium
Detects the WIN_DRV initial-access pattern where a script interpreter creates a scheduled task that subsequently triggers a DLL side-loading chain dropping the named SprySOCKS .dat driver components on the same device within an hour. The temporal join is article-specific and very low FP. Rationale: Article: 'drop a batch script, which then creates and executes a scheduled task responsible for triggering a DLL side-loading chain that drops the SprySOCKS backdoor and the driver components.' Schtasks created by an interpreter, followed within 60 minutes by KW1B/KX1B .dat creation on the SAME device, is article-specific and very low FP — schtasks alone is noisy, the .dat drop alone is already covered by UC1; the temporal join cements article fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1574.002 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR/threat-intel team simultaneously running the malware sample and a scheduled-task hygiene script on a lab VM
  • Patch-management systems creating scheduled tasks coincident with driver-package installs (very rare unless on lab)
  • Backup software creating schtasks and IR analyst dropping the sample on the same machine
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the full process tree for the schtasks creator — what script was it (path, hash, signer); what task name + action XML did it register (DeviceProcessEvents `ProcessCommandLine` carries the full schtasks invocation). Step 2 (contain): isolate the host pre-reboot; collect memory; preserve the dropped .dat and the scheduled-task XML before defenders / responders trigger driver self-defense. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the script hash and the schtasks task-name across the estate; check for the WIN_PLUS sibling chain (spoolsv.exe→svchost.exe and Print Processor registry writes); review for outbound TCP/UDP/WebSocket on the impacted device since SprySOCKS kernel rootkit hides ports — look for unexpected ESTABLISHED sockets in DeviceNetworkEvents.
let SchtasksCreate = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/create", "/Create", "-Create")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
    | project TaskTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName,
              TaskCmd = ProcessCommandLine, TaskParent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
              TaskParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let DriverDrop = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ActionType == "FileCreated"
    | where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^K[WX]1B5206BDC1743(FP|DD)\.dat$"
    | project DropTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DriverFile = FileName, DriverPath = FolderPath,
              DropProc = InitiatingProcessFileName, DropProcCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
SchtasksCreate
| join kind=inner DriverDrop on DeviceId
| where DropTime between (TaskTime .. TaskTime + 1h)
| extend DelayMinutes = datetime_diff('minute', DropTime, TaskTime)
| project TaskTime, DropTime, DelayMinutes, DeviceName, AccountName,
          TaskParent, TaskCmd, DropProc, DropProcCmd, DriverFile, DriverPath
| order by TaskTime desc
let SchtasksCreate = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ActingProcessName has "schtasks.exe"
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/create","/Create","-Create")
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
    | project TaskTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
              TaskCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine, TaskParent = ParentProcessName,
              TaskParentCmd = ParentProcessCommandLine;
let DriverDrop = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EventType == "FileCreated"
    | where TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^K[WX]1B5206BDC1743(FP|DD)\.dat$"
    | project DropTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DriverFile = TargetFileName,
              DriverPath = TargetFilePath, DropProc = ActingProcessName;
SchtasksCreate
| join kind=inner DriverDrop on DvcHostname
| where DropTime between (TaskTime .. TaskTime + 1h)
| extend DelayMinutes = datetime_diff('minute', DropTime, TaskTime)
| project TaskTime, DropTime, DelayMinutes, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TaskParent, TaskCmd, DropProc, DriverFile, DriverPath
| order by TaskTime desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\Schtasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:(*\/create* OR *\/Create* OR *-Create*) @ParentImage:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i CommandLine=/\/(c|C)reate/ ParentBaseFileName=/^(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/(KW1B5206BDC1743FP|KX1B5206BDC1743DD)\.dat$/i}, field=aid, include=[TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine, TargetFileName], function=count(as=ChainHits))
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" Processes.process="*create*" (Processes.parent_process_name="cmd.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="powershell.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="pwsh.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="wscript.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="cscript.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | rename _time as task_time | join type=inner dest [ | tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created (Filesystem.file_name="KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat" OR Filesystem.file_name="KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | rename _time as drop_time dest as dest ] | eval delay_min=round((drop_time-task_time)/60,1) | where delay_min>=0 AND delay_min<=60 | table task_time drop_time delay_min dest user process file_name file_path
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" Processes.process="*create*" (Processes.parent_process_name="cmd.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="powershell.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="pwsh.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="wscript.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="cscript.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | rename _time as task_time | join type=inner dest [ | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created (Filesystem.file_name="KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat" OR Filesystem.file_name="KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | rename _time as drop_time dest as dest ] | eval delay_min=round((drop_time-task_time)/60,1) | where delay_min>=0 AND delay_min<=60 | table task_time drop_time delay_min dest user process file_name file_path
CVE-2023-24932 exposure surface — UEFI bootkit pre-OS attack risk AIWeaponization Medium
Vulnerability-management hunt surfacing Windows hosts unpatched against CVE-2023-24932 (Windows Boot Manager Secure Boot bypass, the BlackLotus UEFI bootkit primitive). The article notes 'limited indications' the FishMonger SprySOCKS campaign may chain a UEFI bootkit using this CVE, so SOC needs to know which hosts are at residual risk. Rationale: Article quote: 'limited indications suggesting the involvement of a UEFI bootkit, likely exploiting CVE-2023-24932... the security flaw was addressed by Microsoft in May 2023.' This hunt surfaces unpatched hosts where the kernel-driver SprySOCKS chain could be paired with a pre-OS bootkit — particularly important on internet-facing hosts (Fortinet/Exchange/Zimbra/GitLab/Telerik are listed as past FishMonger initial-access pivots). Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty as TVM data lives in Defender / vulnerability scanners, not those telemetry sources. Cross-checked against: • https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2023-24932 • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1553.006
Data sourcesVulnerability
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts that have applied the May 2023 patch but where the secondary KB5025885 mitigation (UEFI revocation manifest) has not been deployed — appear vulnerable in TVM even though OS patch is current
  • Recently re-imaged hosts pending policy push
  • Devices with delayed cumulative-update cadence (compliance/regulated workloads)
  • Air-gapped or offline hosts whose TVM data is stale
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): for each host in result set check OS build vs May 2023 cumulative update level and whether the KB5025885 revocations manifest was actually applied (the May patch did NOT auto-enable revocations to avoid bricking dual-boot hosts). Step 2 (contain): prioritise internet-facing and high-value hosts for emergency patch + manifest deployment; for unpatchable hosts apply WDAC bootmgfw/bootmgr code-integrity policy as compensating control. Step 3 (hunt): correlate this list against the SprySOCKS endpoint UCs above — any host appearing here AND in DeviceFileEvents for KW1B/KX1B drops, the kernel-driver-service registration UC, or the spoolsv→svchost UC is a top-priority compromised-asset investigation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId =~ "CVE-2023-24932"
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId, CveId
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceInfo
    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId
    | project DeviceId, IsInternetFacing, JoinType, MachineGroup, PublicIP, LoggedOnUsers
  ) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, RecommendedSecurityUpdateId,
          IsInternetFacing, JoinType, MachineGroup, PublicIP, LoggedOnUsers
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, Timestamp desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

Dozens of malicious wallpapers found on Steam Workshop: gamers’ accounts at risk

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-06-16 14 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Since late 2025, malware has been spreading rapidly through the Steam Workshop, the gaming platform's built-in service for players to create and share custom content. The attackers are primarily targeting gamers in China and Russia.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Wallpaper Engine spawning script interpreters or LOLBins from workshop content · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Dozens of malicious wallpapers found on Steam Workshop: gamers’ accounts at risk
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Wallpaper Engine spawning Synaptics.exe or ._cache_GAME1.exe (Steam Workshop wallpaper malware) · [LLM] Trojanized AggregatorHost.dll dropped outside System32 (Steam credential-stealer DLL) · [LLM] IOC hash match — Steam Workshop wallpaper malware MD5 bundle · [LLM] Persistence via Run key referencing Wallpaper Engine / Synaptics / NTRaholic paths · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] C2 callback to Steam Workshop wallpaper campaign infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Wallpaper Engine spawning Synaptics.exe or ._cache_GAME1.exe (Steam Workshop wallpaper malware) AIInstallation High
Detects the specific child-process chain described in the Kaspersky writeup where the Wallpaper Engine host binary (wallpaper32/64.exe) launches the malicious Synaptics.exe (DarkKomet) backdoor or the ._cache_GAME1.exe dropper bundled inside compromised Steam Workshop application wallpapers. Both filenames are taken verbatim from the article. Rationale: Article explicitly names 'Synaptics.exe' (DarkKomet family) and '._cache_GAME1.exe' as the dropper pair installed by the malicious wallpaper. Parent process is Wallpaper Engine (wallpaper32/64.exe per reviewer feedback). This combination is unique to the documented Steam Workshop campaign and matches no known benign software. Cross-checked against: • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.dark_komet
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Wallpaper Engine 'application' wallpapers that happen to launch a bundled game named NTRaholic from a non-malicious workshop entry (rare but possible if the Synaptics naming clashes with a legitimate Synaptics touchpad utility located in the same path)
  • Synaptics touchpad driver updater (SynTPEnh.exe / Synaptics.exe) genuinely installed by an OEM in C:\Program Files\Synaptics — distinguishable by signed publisher and parent svchost.exe, not wallpaper32.exe
  • Wallpaper Engine internal cache files matching ._cache_* pattern from non-malicious workshop content (the GAME1.exe suffix is the distinguishing token)
  • Red-team simulation using publicly-published IOCs from the Kaspersky article
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files\Synaptics\" and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Synaptics")
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Pull the full process tree for the alert — confirm parent is wallpaper32/64.exe and capture the SHA256 of the child Synaptics.exe / ._cache_GAME1.exe. Compare hash against the 13 MD5 IOC bundle in the article. Check DeviceFileEvents for which workshop subscription ID dropped the file (path under \Steam\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\). 2. CONTAIN: Isolate the host via Defender Live Response, kill wallpaper32/64.exe and Synaptics.exe processes, quarantine the dropped binaries, and force-logout the user's Steam session by rotating the password and revoking sessions via Steam Support. 3. HUNT: Search the org for other downloads from the same Steam Workshop entry, pivot on the SHA256 across DeviceFileEvents, and check DeviceNetworkEvents for the C2 IPs 120.48.156.17 and 202.144.192.29.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe","webwallpaper32.exe","webwallpaper64.exe","wallpaperservice32_c.exe","wallpaperservice64_c.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("Synaptics.exe","_cache_GAME1.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Synaptics.exe","._cache_GAME1.exe","NTRaholic")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(web)?wallpaper(32|64)(_c)?\.exe$" or ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\wallpaperservice(32|64)_c\.exe$"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(Synaptics|_cache_GAME1)\.exe$"
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Synaptics.exe","._cache_GAME1.exe","NTRaholic")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: Detects Wallpaper Engine host binary launching Synaptics.exe (DarkKomet) or ._cache_GAME1.exe dropper bundled inside malicious Steam Workshop application wallpapers.

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/(web)?wallpaper(32|64)(_c)?\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(Synaptics|_cache_GAME1)\.exe$/i OR CommandLine=/Synaptics\.exe|_cache_GAME1\.exe|NTRaholic/i

Trojanized AggregatorHost.dll dropped outside System32 (Steam credential-stealer DLL) AIInstallation High
The article describes a custom AggregatorHost.dll that impersonates the legitimate Windows system DLL and is used to hijack the Steam session. The genuine file ships only inside %SystemRoot%\System32. Any AggregatorHost.dll written to user-writable locations (Steam directories, Wallpaper Engine workshop subdirs, %TEMP%, %APPDATA%) is an immediate red flag. Rationale: Article: 'installs a custom version of a system library called AggregatorHost.dll with a payload inside' — the malicious DLL impersonates the legit Windows file. Any drop outside System32/SysWOW64/WinSxS is anomalous because Windows never relocates that DLL. High-fidelity name+location anomaly.
ATT&CKT1574.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows servicing operations (DISM, WUSA) temporarily staging system DLLs in %TEMP%\WinSxS-staging during cumulative updates — distinguishable by parent TiWorker.exe/TrustedInstaller.exe
  • Endpoint imaging tools (SCCM, Intune) restoring System32 contents to a backup directory during repair operations
  • Symbol-server caches where a developer copied the file for debugging into a tools directory
  • Red-team simulation using the public IOC bundle
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TiWorker.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","wusa.exe","DISM.exe")
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Hash the dropped AggregatorHost.dll and compare against the legitimate copy at %SystemRoot%\System32\AggregatorHost.dll (file signing certificate is Microsoft Windows Publisher). Check the dropping process — if InitiatingProcessFileName is wallpaper32/64.exe or a process under \Steam\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\, treat as confirmed. 2. CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill any process with that DLL mapped (use DeviceImageLoadEvents pivot), quarantine the file, and rotate the user's Steam credentials and active session tokens. 3. HUNT: Pivot the DLL SHA256 across the fleet and look for outbound traffic to 120.48.156.17/ey.php — the trojanized DLL exfils Steam session data to that endpoint.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName =~ "AggregatorHost.dll"
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\System32\", @"\Windows\SysWOW64\", @"\Windows\WinSxS\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName =~ "AggregatorHost.dll"
| where not (TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Windows\System32\", @"\Windows\SysWOW64\", @"\Windows\WinSxS\"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, TargetFileMD5, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 callback to Steam Workshop wallpaper campaign infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections to the two C2 endpoints named in the article (120.48.156.17 hosting /ey.php for Steam session exfil, 202.144.192.29 hosting /audit.php and /download2/Themes2.zip) or to the brightly.to domain. Captures both IP literal hits and URL-based requests. Rationale: Article verbatim: 'sends all the collected data to a server controlled by the hackers at hxxp://120.48.156[.]17/ey.php' and the IOC block lists http://202.144.192[.]29/audit.php plus http://202.144.192[.]29/download2/Themes2.zip. brightly.to is in the pre-extracted IOCs. Specific IP+URI pairs make this near-zero FP.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst sandbox detonating the same samples and triggering the same callbacks — should be allow-listed by sandbox hostname
  • Security researcher pivoting on the IOCs via curl/wget for verification — distinguishable by user-agent and originating analyst workstation
  • Internal IP-reputation scanner probing the published IOC bundle as part of validation
  • Stale CTI feed pulling the IOC list via HTTP (the feed processor itself reaches the IPs)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\sandbox\"
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Identify the host and InitiatingProcessFileName making the connection. If parent is wallpaper32/64.exe, Synaptics.exe, or any process under a Steam workshop directory, treat as confirmed campaign hit. Pull the matching DeviceProcessEvents 5 minutes either side to reconstruct the chain. 2. CONTAIN: Block 120.48.156.17 and 202.144.192.29 at the egress firewall and DNS sinkhole brightly.to. Isolate the host, rotate the user's Steam credentials, and revoke active Steam Web API tokens. 3. HUNT: Pivot the SHA256 of the calling process across the fleet, hash-match all 13 MD5s from the IOC bundle in DeviceFileEvents over 30d, and check whether the user's Steam account was used to publish any new Workshop entries (campaign self-propagation pattern described in article).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("120.48.156.17","202.144.192.29")
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("ey.php","audit.php","download2/Themes2.zip","brightly.to")
   or RemoteUrl has "120.48.156.17"
   or RemoteUrl has "202.144.192.29"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("120.48.156.17","202.144.192.29")
   or Url has_any ("ey.php","audit.php","download2/Themes2.zip","brightly.to","120.48.156.17","202.144.192.29")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, SrcUsername, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

IOC hash match — Steam Workshop wallpaper malware MD5 bundle AIInstallation Medium
Hash-based detection for the 13 MD5s published in the Kaspersky IOC bundle. Catches the binaries across process execution, file creation, and parent-process telemetry — gives broad surface coverage even if the campaign rotates filenames and parent process trees. Rationale: 13 MD5 hashes are verbatim from the article's IOC block. Hashing across DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceFileEvents, and DeviceImageLoadEvents catches the dropper, the DarkKomet payload, the trojanized AggregatorHost.dll, and any future variants reusing the same binaries even if filenames are rotated.
ATT&CKT1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst sandbox executing the samples for triage
  • EDR product itself replaying historical alerts that reference these hashes during testing
  • Threat-intel platform staging the hashes locally for indicator validation
  • Red-team exercise using the published IOC bundle
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Confirm the hit is not from a known sandbox / analyst workstation (check `DeviceInfo.MachineGroup`). Capture file path and parent process tree. 2. CONTAIN: Quarantine the file via Defender Live Response, isolate the host, kill any running processes matching the SHA256, and rotate Steam credentials for the logged-on user. 3. HUNT: Use the SHA256 from this hit to back-trace the dropping process; check if the file came from \steamapps\workshop\content\431960\ (the Wallpaper Engine workshop app ID) — if so, identify the workshop subscription IDs and check fleet-wide for the same downloads.

union

     | where Timestamp > ago(30d)

     | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source="Process", Path=FolderPath, FileName, MD5, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine),

     | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="ImageLoad", Path=FolderPath, FileName, MD5, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc

Wallpaper Engine spawning script interpreters or LOLBins from workshop content AIExploitation Medium
Broader hunting query for the 'application wallpaper' execution model described in the article — Wallpaper Engine launches user-supplied executables that may chain to cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe, rundll32.exe, or other interpreters. Application wallpapers from Steam Workshop should never legitimately need a script interpreter; this hunts the entire campaign pattern beyond the specific Synaptics/cache_GAME1 filenames. Rationale: Article: 'Application wallpapers are essentially standalone programs' and 'allows foreign code to be run directly on your computer'. Wallpaper Engine itself has no legitimate need to spawn cmd/powershell/wscript — these parent-child pairs are a clean campaign indicator. Catches variants that don't reuse the Synaptics/_cache_GAME1 names from UC1.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Wallpaper Engine 'Workshop' page launch invoking rundll32.exe for Windows shell preview thumbnails (rare but possible on first-time workshop browsing)
  • Legitimate scene wallpaper using a small PowerShell helper to query system stats (e.g., custom CPU/GPU monitor widget) — should be allow-listed by SHA256 of the workshop entry
  • Wallpaper Engine config repair launching cmd.exe to flush a corrupted cache
  • Steam Big Picture mode launching wallpaper through a shell wrapper
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--update-check","--repair-cache","thumbnail"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Pull the full command line — if it contains base64-encoded PowerShell, references a URL, or drops anything to %TEMP%/%APPDATA%, treat as confirmed. Hash the parent .exe (the workshop application wallpaper) and check against the IOC bundle. 2. CONTAIN: Suspend wallpaper32/64.exe, kill child processes, isolate host, snapshot \Steam\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\ subscription directories for forensic analysis. 3. HUNT: Identify the workshop subscription ID and check whether other users in the org downloaded the same wallpaper — pivot on the workshop folder GUID across DeviceFileEvents.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe","webwallpaper32.exe","webwallpaper64.exe","wallpaperservice32_c.exe","wallpaperservice64_c.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
   or (FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Users\Public\") and FileName endswith ".exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(web)?wallpaper(32|64)(_c)?\.exe$" or ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\wallpaperservice(32|64)_c\.exe$"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|bitsadmin|certutil|curl|wget)\.exe$"
   or ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(AppData\\Local\\Temp|AppData\\Roaming|Users\\Public)\\[^\\]+\.exe$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

  - attack.t1059.003

  product: windows
detection:

      - '\wallpaper32.exe'
      - '\wallpaper64.exe'
      - '\webwallpaper32.exe'

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe","webwallpaper32.exe","webwallpaper64.exe") AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe") by host Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

Persistence via Run key referencing Wallpaper Engine / Synaptics / NTRaholic paths AIInstallation Medium
Detects autostart registry writes (Run / RunOnce / Image File Execution Options) that reference the artifacts named in the Kaspersky article — Synaptics.exe outside the legit Synaptics folder, ._cache_GAME1.exe, or any value pointing into \steamapps\workshop\content\431960\ (Wallpaper Engine's workshop directory). DarkKomet's classic Run-key persistence anchored to this campaign's specific filenames. Rationale: Article: 'leave the victim's system infected with backdoors or crypto miners' — backdoors persist. DarkKomet's documented behavior is Run-key persistence, and the article names Synaptics.exe and ._cache_GAME1.exe as the dropped artifacts. Filtering out the legitimate Synaptics touchpad driver path keeps FP rate low.
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Synaptics touchpad driver Run key (HKCU\...\Run\SynTPEnh) — excluded by the \Program Files\Synaptics\ path filter
  • Steam itself registering a Run key referencing steamapps directory for game updaters
  • Wallpaper Engine adding its own Run key during install (under \Wallpaper Engine\wallpaper32.exe, NOT under \workshop\content\)
  • User manually adding NTRaholic to startup after legitimately installing the game from another source
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("steam.exe","steamservice.exe") or RegistryValueData !has @"\steamapps\common\"
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Inspect the InitiatingProcessFileName that wrote the registry value — if it's wallpaper32/64.exe, Synaptics.exe (outside the legit Synaptics directory), or ._cache_GAME1.exe, treat as confirmed. Capture the value data path and verify the binary exists. 2. CONTAIN: Delete the registry value, quarantine the file at the referenced path, kill any running instances, and isolate the host. Rotate the user's Steam password and revoke active sessions. 3. HUNT: Pivot the file SHA256 across DeviceProcessEvents to find first execution, check DeviceNetworkEvents for 120.48.156.17/202.144.192.29 callbacks, and hash-match all 13 IOCs across the fleet to find other infected endpoints.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce", @"\Image File Execution Options\", @"\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Shell", @"\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Userinit")
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("Synaptics.exe","_cache_GAME1.exe","NTRaholic",@"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\")
| where not (RegistryValueData has @"\Program Files\Synaptics\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce", @"\Image File Execution Options\", @"\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Shell", @"\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Userinit")
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("Synaptics.exe","_cache_GAME1.exe","NTRaholic",@"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\")
| where not (RegistryValueData has @"\Program Files\Synaptics\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

title: Run Key Persistence Referencing Steam Workshop Wallpaper Malware Artifacts
id: 6a3f9c1d-4e8b-4d7f-b0a2-9c1d2e5f8b77
status: experimental
description: Autostart registry value written that references Synaptics.exe (outside legit Synaptics path), ._cache_GAME1.exe, NTRaholic, or the Wallpaper Engine workshop content directory.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/dozens-of-malicious-wallpapers-found-on-steam-workshop/120186/
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.t1547.001
logsource:
  category: registry_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_key:
    TargetObject|contains:
      - '\CurrentVersion\Run\'
      - '\CurrentVersion\RunOnce\'
      - '\Image File Execution Options\'
      - '\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Shell'
      - '\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Userinit'
  selection_data:
    Details|contains:
      - 'Synaptics.exe'
      - '_cache_GAME1.exe'
      - 'NTRaholic'
      - '\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\'
  filter_legit_synaptics:
    Details|contains: '\Program Files\Synaptics\'
  condition: selection_key and selection_data and not filter_legit_synaptics
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:13 @TargetObject:(*\CurrentVersion\Run\* OR *\CurrentVersion\RunOnce\* OR *\Image File Execution Options\* OR *\currentversion\run\* OR *\currentversion\runonce\*) @Details:(*Synaptics.exe* OR *synaptics.exe* OR *_cache_GAME1.exe* OR *_cache_game1.exe* OR *NTRaholic* OR *ntraholic* OR *\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\*) -@Details:(*\Program Files\Synaptics\* OR *\program files\synaptics\*)
#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate
| RegObjectName=/\\CurrentVersion\\(Run|RunOnce)\\|\\Image File Execution Options\\|\\Winlogon\\(Shell|Userinit)/i
| RegStringValue=/Synaptics\.exe|_cache_GAME1\.exe|NTRaholic|\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\/i
| NOT RegStringValue=/\\Program Files\\Synaptics\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RegObjectName, RegValueName, RegStringValue, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path IN ("*\\CurrentVersion\\Run\\*","*\\CurrentVersion\\RunOnce\\*","*\\CurrentVersion\\Image File Execution Options\\*") AND (Registry.registry_value_data="*Synaptics.exe*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*_cache_GAME1.exe*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*NTRaholic*") by host Registry.user Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data Registry.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path IN ("*\\CurrentVersion\\Run\\*","*\\CurrentVersion\\RunOnce\\*","*\\CurrentVersion\\Image File Execution Options\\*") AND (Registry.registry_value_data="*Synaptics.exe*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*_cache_GAME1.exe*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*NTRaholic*") by host Registry.user Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data Registry.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High

ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("202.144.192.29", "120.48.156.17") or RemoteUrl has_any ("brightly.to")

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
